1	---
2	title: "CellTFusion"
3	output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
4	vignette: >
5	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{CellTFusion}
6	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
7	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
8	---
9	
10	```{r, include = FALSE}
11	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
12	  collapse = TRUE,
13	  comment = "#>"
14	)
15	```
16	
17	`CellTFusion` integrates immune cell type deconvolution with transcription factor (TF)–gene regulatory networks to characterize immune cell states in the tumor microenvironment (TME) from bulk RNA-seq data.
18	
19	Starting from a count matrix, `CellTFusion` builds **cell groups** — sets of deconvolution features related to the same TF co-activity module to the same degree (a similar correlation with the module activity) — and summarizes them into **latent factors**, a compact representation of the TME that can be annotated as TME states, tested against clinical variables and used as features for machine learning.
20	
21	## Installation
22	
23	To avoid GitHub API rate limit issues, set up a Personal Access Token (PAT) before installing:
24	
25	```{r, eval = FALSE}
26	# install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
27	usethis::create_github_token()
28	gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
29	```
30	
31	Install `CellTFusion` from GitHub:
32	
33	```{r, eval = FALSE}
34	# install.packages("pak")
35	pak::pkg_install("VeraPancaldiLab/CellTFusion")
36	```
37	
38	## Quick start
39	
40	The `CellTFusion()` wrapper runs the whole pipeline in one call, using the example data shipped with the package. Intermediate results and plots are saved in a `Results/` folder in the working directory.
41	
42	```{r, eval = FALSE}
43	library(CellTFusion)
44	
45	res <- CellTFusion(
46	  raw_counts     = CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto,
47	  normalized     = TRUE,
48	  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
49	  file_name      = "Tutorial"
50	)
51	
52	head(res$Latent_spaces$Z)  # latent factor scores (samples x factors)
53	```
54	
55	## Pipeline
56	
57	| Step | Function | Tutorial |
58	| --- | --- | --- |
59	| Cell type deconvolution | `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
60	| TF activity inference | `compute.TFs.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
61	| TF co-activity modules | `compute.WTCNA()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
62	| Pathway activity | `compute.pathway.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
63	| Cell groups | `construct_cell_groups()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
64	| Latent factors | `compute.latent_factors()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
65	| Cell niches | `compute_cells_niches()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
66	| Clinical associations | `scores.stat.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
67	| Survival analysis | `compute.survival.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
68	| Cross-validation with `pipeML` | `prepare_celltfusion_folds()` | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
69	| Projection of new cohorts | `compute.test.set()` (cell groups), `project_factors()` (latent factors) | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
70	| Multi-cohort analysis | `CellTFusion(batch = ...)` | [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html) |
71	
72	## Tutorials
73	
74	Step-by-step tutorials are available in the **Articles** section of the navigation bar:
75	
76	- **[Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html)** — cell type deconvolution, TF activity, TF co-activity modules and pathway activity
77	- **[Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html)** — build cell groups, extract latent factors and characterize cell niches
78	- **[Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html)** — associations with clinical variables and survival
79	- **[Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html)** — use cell group scores as features and score independent cohorts
80	- **[Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)** — correct for cohort effects with `batch`
81	
82	## Shiny app
83	
84	`CellTFusion` includes an interactive app to run the pipeline on the example data or on your own data:
85	
86	```{r, eval = FALSE}
87	shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "CellTFusion"))
88	```
89	
90	## Citation
91	
92	If you use `CellTFusion` in a scientific publication, please cite:
93	
94	> Hurtado, M., & Pancaldi, V. (2026). *CellTFusion: A transcriptional regulatory network framework for the identification of functional multicellular states from bulk RNA-seq data.* bioRxiv. <https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.06.30.735682>
95

file.content:
---
title: "CellTFusion"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{CellTFusion}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

`CellTFusion` integrates immune cell type deconvolution with transcription factor (TF)–gene regulatory networks to characterize immune cell states in the tumor microenvironment (TME) from bulk RNA-seq data.

Starting from a count matrix, `CellTFusion` builds **cell groups** — sets of deconvolution features related to the same TF co-activity module to the same degree (a similar correlation with the module activity) — and summarizes them into **latent factors**, a compact representation of the TME that can be annotated as TME states, tested against clinical variables and used as features for machine learning.

## Installation

To avoid GitHub API rate limit issues, set up a Personal Access Token (PAT) before installing:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
usethis::create_github_token()
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Install `CellTFusion` from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("VeraPancaldiLab/CellTFusion")
```

## Quick start

The `CellTFusion()` wrapper runs the whole pipeline in one call, using the example data shipped with the package. Intermediate results and plots are saved in a `Results/` folder in the working directory.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(CellTFusion)

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto,
  normalized     = TRUE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
  file_name      = "Tutorial"
)

head(res$Latent_spaces$Z)  # latent factor scores (samples x factors)
```

## Pipeline

| Step | Function | Tutorial |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cell type deconvolution | `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| TF activity inference | `compute.TFs.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| TF co-activity modules | `compute.WTCNA()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| Pathway activity | `compute.pathway.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| Cell groups | `construct_cell_groups()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
| Latent factors | `compute.latent_factors()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
| Cell niches | `compute_cells_niches()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
| Clinical associations | `scores.stat.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
| Survival analysis | `compute.survival.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
| Cross-validation with `pipeML` | `prepare_celltfusion_folds()` | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
| Projection of new cohorts | `compute.test.set()` (cell groups), `project_factors()` (latent factors) | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
| Multi-cohort analysis | `CellTFusion(batch = ...)` | [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html) |

## Tutorials

Step-by-step tutorials are available in the **Articles** section of the navigation bar:

- **[Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html)** — cell type deconvolution, TF activity, TF co-activity modules and pathway activity
- **[Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html)** — build cell groups, extract latent factors and characterize cell niches
- **[Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html)** — associations with clinical variables and survival
- **[Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html)** — use cell group scores as features and score independent cohorts
- **[Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)** — correct for cohort effects with `batch`

## Shiny app

`CellTFusion` includes an interactive app to run the pipeline on the example data or on your own data:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "CellTFusion"))
```

## Citation

If you use `CellTFusion` in a scientific publication, please cite:

> Hurtado, M., & Pancaldi, V. (2026). *CellTFusion: A transcriptional regulatory network framework for the identification of functional multicellular states from bulk RNA-seq data.* bioRxiv. <https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.06.30.735682>

44	)
45	}
46	\arguments{
47	\item{raw_counts}{A matrix of raw gene expression counts (genes as rows, samples as columns). If
48	\code{normalized = FALSE}, a matrix of TPM-normalized values instead (not log-transformed).
49	Always required, also when \code{dt}, \code{tfs} and \code{pathways} are all supplied precomputed (its samples
50	are checked against them).}
51	
52	\item{deconv}{(Optional) A data frame with deconvolution features (cell-type proportions as columns x samples as rows).
53	If \code{NULL} (default), it is computed with \code{multideconv::compute.deconvolution()} using
54	\code{deconv_methods}. Ignored if \code{dt} is supplied.}
55	
56	\item{dt}{(Optional) A precomputed cell-subgroup object, typically the output of
57	\code{multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()} (or the \code{Processed_deconvolution} element
58	returned by a previous \code{CellTFusion()} run). If supplied, cell-type deconvolution and the
59	deconvolution analysis step are both skipped and the pipeline proceeds straight to cell group
60	construction using this object. It must have the same samples as \code{raw_counts}.}
61	
62	\item{tfs}{(Optional) A precomputed TF activity matrix (samples as rows, TFs as columns), typically
63	the \code{TFs_matrix} element returned by a previous \code{CellTFusion()} run or by
64	\code{compute.TFs.activity()}. When \code{batch} is given, a named list of such matrices (one per cohort).
65	If supplied, TF activity inference is skipped.}
66	
67	\item{pathways}{(Optional) A precomputed pathway activity matrix, typically the \code{Pathways_scores}
68	element returned by a previous \code{CellTFusion()} run or by \code{compute.pathway.activity()}.
69	If supplied, pathway activity inference is skipped.}
70	
71	\item{normalized}{Logical; if TRUE (default), \code{raw_counts} are raw counts and are normalized to
72	log2(TPM + 1) for the TF activity and pathway activity steps (for deconvolution they are normalized to
73	TPM only). If FALSE, \code{raw_counts} must already be TPM-normalized and \strong{not} log-transformed: the
74	TPM values are used as they are for deconvolution and log2(TPM + 1) is computed internally for the other
75	steps. Do not pass log-transformed values, as they would be log-transformed a second time (a warning is
76	given when the values do not look like TPM, i.e. no value above 20 or negative values).}
77	
78	\item{batch}{(Optional) A vector with the cohort of each sample (e.g. \code{coldata$Cohort}), in the same order
79	as the columns of \code{raw_counts}; if it is named, it is matched to the samples by name instead. It is
80	always treated as categorical. If given, the multi-cohort mode is run: TF and pathway activities are computed per
81	cohort, TF modules are built from a consensus network across cohorts (see \code{consensus_quantile}), and the cohort is controlled for in the
82	deconvolution analysis and cell group construction. Default is \code{NULL} (single cohort); a vector with
83	only one cohort is treated the same way.}
84	
85	\item{deconv_methods}{A character vector of deconvolution methods to apply. Default is
86	\code{c("Quantiseq", "CBSX", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS")}. \code{"CBSX"} (CIBERSORTx) is only run
87	when \code{cbsx_mail} and \code{cbsx_token} are given; otherwise it is skipped with a message.}
88	
89	\item{cbsx_mail}{(Optional) Email credential for CIBERSORTx. Needed to run "CBSX"; without it, CIBERSORTx is skipped.}
90	
91	\item{cbsx_token}{(Optional) Token credential for CIBERSORTx. Needed to run "CBSX"; without it, CIBERSORTx is skipped.}
92	
93	\item{do_parallel}{Logical; whether to run the deconvolution methods that support it (CIBERSORTx and DWLS) in
94	parallel, one signature per worker (passed to \code{multideconv::compute.deconvolution()} as \code{doParallel}). Default is FALSE.}
95	
96	\item{workers}{(Optional) Number of parallel workers when \code{do_parallel = TRUE}. If \code{NULL} (default),
97	the number of available cores minus one is used.}
98	
99	\item{file_name}{(Optional) Name used in the output files saved in the "Results/" directory. If \code{NULL}
100	and \code{return = TRUE}, \code{"CellTFusion"} is used.}
101	
102	\item{TF.collection}{Character. The source of the TF-target network. Options are \code{"CollecTRI"} (default), \code{"Dorothea"}, or \code{"ARACNE"}.
103	\itemize{
104	\item \code{"CollecTRI"} uses the prebuilt collection from OmnipathR and \code{"Dorothea"} the one from the \code{dorothea} package.
105	\item \code{"ARACNE"} reads a network file (tab-separated with \code{Regulator} and \code{Target} columns, and a \code{mor} column with
106	the sign of each interaction; see \code{compute.TFs.activity()}) from
107	\code{input/ARACNE/<cancer_type>/network/network.txt}.
108	}}
109	
110	\item{method}{Character. The \code{decoupleR} statistic used to score the TFs and the PROGENy pathways: \code{"ulm"}
111	(univariate linear model, default), \code{"mlm"} (multivariate linear model), \code{"wsum"} (weighted sum) or
112	\code{"consensus"} (consensus of the three). Passed to \code{compute.TFs.activity()} and \code{compute.pathway.activity()}.}
113	
114	\item{min_targets_size}{Integer. Minimum number of target genes per regulon, passed to
115	\code{compute.TFs.activity()}. Default is 5.}
116	
117	\item{universe}{Optional. A user-specified data frame of TF-target interactions (columns \code{source}, \code{target} and
118	\code{mor}, the mode of regulation: 1 activation, -1 repression). If not provided, the function will fetch the relevant network based on the \code{TF.collection} argument.}
119	
120	\item{paths}{Optional. A user-specified data frame of pathways gene sets. If not provided, the function will fetch the relevant pathways based on \code{PROGENy}.}
121	
122	\item{gene_sets}{Optional. A named list of custom gene sets (character vectors of gene symbols) passed to
123	\code{compute.pathway.activity()}'s \code{gene_sets} argument for GSVA-based scoring. If \code{NULL}, only PROGENy is used.}
124	
125	\item{min_module_size}{Integer; minimum module size for WGCNA module detection. Default is 5.}
126	
127	\item{corr_mod}{Numeric; correlation threshold for merging TF modules. Default is 0.9.}
128	
129	\item{soft_power}{(Optional) Soft-thresholding power used to build the TF network, passed to

content.content:
# TME state characterization

``` r
library(CellTFusion)
#> 
```

Once latent factors have been extracted (see [Cell groups and latent
factors](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a2_cell_groups.md)),
each factor can be linked to known biological programs:

1.  **Hallmark GSEA** — associate each factor with MSigDB Hallmark gene
    sets.
2.  **Meta-program mapping** — match each factor to cancer type-specific
    reference programs derived from TCGA.
3.  **TME subtype annotation** — relate factors to established TME
    subtypes.

These steps use:

- `counts.norm` — normalized expression matrix (genes x samples).
- `latent_spaces` — output of
  [`compute.latent_factors()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute.latent_factors.md);
  `latent_spaces$Z` is the samples x factors matrix.

## **Hallmark GSEA per latent factor**

[`compute_factor_gsea()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute_factor_gsea.md)
fits a multivariate `limma` model with the latent factor scores as
covariates, ranks genes by their moderated t-statistic for each factor,
and runs a pre-ranked GSEA with `fgsea` ([Korotkevich et al.
2021](#ref-Korotkevich2021)) against the MSigDB Hallmark collection
([Liberzon et al. 2015](#ref-Liberzon2015)). The Hallmark collection
summarizes about 50 well-defined biological processes (e.g. EMT,
interferon response, hypoxia), a natural vocabulary to interpret
data-driven factors. The samples of `features_df` must be in the same
order as the columns of `RNA.tpm`.

``` r
gsea_results <- compute_factor_gsea(
  RNA.tpm     = counts.norm,
  features_df = latent_spaces$Z,
  plot_dot    = TRUE,
  top_n       = 10,
  file_name   = "Tutorial"
)
```

| Element         | Description                                   |
|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `$DE_results`   | Named list of `limma` results, one per factor |
| `$GSEA_results` | Named list of `fgsea` results, one per factor |

With `plot_dot = TRUE`, a dot plot of the top Hallmarks is saved per
factor (dot size = significance, color = normalized enrichment score,
NES):

![Dot plot of the top Hallmark gene sets for latent factor
1](figures/gsea_factor1.png)

## **Mapping factors to TCGA meta-programs**

### What are meta-programs?

A **meta-program (MP)** is a recurrent transcriptional program
reflecting a cell state (e.g. cell cycle, hypoxia,
epithelial-mesenchymal transition, interferon response) that recurs
across tumors and cancer types. Gavish et al. ([Gavish et al.
2023](#ref-Gavish2023)) characterized such programs from single-cell
RNA-seq across many cancers. `CellTFusion` follows the same logic with
bulk TCGA data: it derives cancer type-specific meta-programs from TCGA,
so that factors found in a new study can be described with a shared
vocabulary of TME states.

### How `map_factors_to_metaprograms()` works

1.  **Reference (pre-built, per cancer type):** `CellTFusion` was run on
    a TCGA cohort, and the Hallmarks were clustered by their NES
    profiles across the TCGA factors
    ([`derive_meta_programs()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/derive_meta_programs.md)).
    Each resulting meta-program is a set of Hallmarks, annotated with a
    TME subtype (see below). References are shipped for `"blca"`
    (bladder cancer), `"luad"` (lung adenocarcinoma) and `"skcm"`
    (melanoma).
2.  **Study factors:** the Hallmark NES of each study factor come from
    [`compute_factor_gsea()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute_factor_gsea.md).
3.  **Matching:** for each study factor and each meta-program, the mean
    NES of the meta-program’s Hallmarks is computed. The meta-program
    with the highest positive mean NES is the factor’s `best_MP`.

In other words: *which known program does this factor’s Hallmark
signature resemble most?*

``` r
mp_mapping <- map_factors_to_metaprograms(
  gsea_study  = gsea_results,
  cancer_type = "skcm",
  plot        = TRUE,
  file_name   = "Tutorial"
)
```

| Element           | Description                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `$factor_mapping` | One row per study factor: `factor`, `best_MP`, `best_score` (its mean NES), `all_scores` (mean NES for every meta-program) and `TME_subtype` of the best meta-program |
| `$reference`      | The meta-program reference: `meta_program`, its `hallmarks` and `TME_subtype`                                                                                         |

A custom reference can be used with `mp_file`, either a data frame like
`$reference` or the path to an `.RData` file containing an object named
`meta_programs`.

With `plot = TRUE`, each panel shows a study factor: grey bars are the
mean NES for every meta-program, and the best-matching one is colored by
its TME subtype:

![Bar plots of mean NES per meta-program for each study factor, with the
best match highlighted](figures/mp_mapping.png)

## **TME subtypes**

[`map_factors_to_TME()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/map_factors_to_TME.md)
uses the TCGA annotations of Bagaev et al. ([Bagaev et al.
2021](#ref-Bagaev2021)), who defined four pan-cancer TME subtypes
(Molecular Functional Portraits, MFP):

- **IE** (immune-enriched, non-fibrotic) — high immune infiltration, low
  stromal signal.
- **IE/F** (immune-enriched, fibrotic) — high immune infiltration with a
  fibrotic/stromal signature.
- **F** (fibrotic) — stroma-dominated, low immune infiltration.
- **D** (depleted) — low immune infiltration and low fibrosis.

These subtypes are associated with response to immune checkpoint
blockade. For a TCGA cancer type,
[`map_factors_to_TME()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/map_factors_to_TME.md)
matches the TCGA patients in `Z` to their MFP subtype and tests each
factor across the four subtypes with a Kruskal-Wallis test. Factors with
p \< 0.05 are labeled with the subtype that has the highest median
score; the others are labeled `"uncharacterized"`. This is how the TME
subtypes of the TCGA meta-program references were assigned
([`annotate_metaprograms_TME()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/annotate_metaprograms_TME.md)).

``` r
tme_annotation <- map_factors_to_TME(
  cancer_name = "skcm",
  Z           = latent_spaces$Z,   # TCGA samples x factors
  plot        = TRUE,
  file_name   = "Tutorial"
)
```

## **Deriving meta-programs**

To build your own reference, for example from several cohorts,
[`derive_meta_programs()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/derive_meta_programs.md)
clusters the Hallmarks by their NES profiles across factors. The number
of meta-programs `k` is chosen at the elbow of the within-cluster sum of
squares if `NULL`.

``` r
meta_programs <- derive_meta_programs(
  gsea_results = gsea_results,
  k            = NULL,
  file_name    = "Tutorial",
  plot         = TRUE
)
```

## **Running everything with `CellTFusion()`**

The GSEA and meta-program mapping are run by
[`CellTFusion()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/CellTFusion.md)
when `cancer_type` is given:

``` r
res <- CellTFusion(raw.counts = raw.counts, cancer_type = "skcm")

res$TME_states              # factor-to-meta-program mapping
res$Metaprograms_reference  # meta-program reference used
```

## References

Bagaev, Alexander, Nikita Kotlov, Krystle Nomie, Viktor Svekolkin,
Azamat Gafurov, Olga Isaeva, Nikita Osokin, et al. 2021. “Conserved
Pan-Cancer Microenvironment Subtypes Predict Response to Immunotherapy.”
*Cancer Cell* 39 (6): 845–865.e7.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccell.2021.04.014>.

Gavish, Avishai, Michael Tyler, Alissa C. Greenwald, Rouven Hoefflin,
Dor Simkin, Roman Tschernichovsky, Noam Galili Darnell, et al. 2023.
“Hallmarks of Transcriptional Intratumour Heterogeneity Across a
Thousand Tumours.” *Nature* 618 (7965): 598–606.
<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06130-4>.

Korotkevich, Gennady, Vladimir Sukhov, Nikolay Budin, Boris Shpak, Maxim
N. Artyomov, and Alexey Sergushichev. 2021. “Fast Gene Set Enrichment
Analysis.” *bioRxiv*. <https://doi.org/10.1101/060012>.

Liberzon, Arthur, Chet Birger, Helga Thorvaldsdóttir, Mahmoud Ghandi,
Jill P. Mesirov, and Pablo Tamayo. 2015. “The Molecular Signatures
Database (MSigDB) Hallmark Gene Set Collection.” *Cell Systems* 1 (6):
417–25. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cels.2015.12.004>.

``` r
  plot        = TRUE,
  file_name   = "Tutorial"
)
```

## **Deriving meta-programs**

To build your own reference, for example from several cohorts,
[`derive_meta_programs()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/derive_meta_programs.md)
clusters the Hallmarks by their NES profiles across factors. The number
of meta-programs `k` is chosen at the elbow of the within-cluster sum of
squares if `NULL`.

``` r
meta_programs <- derive_meta_programs(
  gsea_results = gsea_results,
  k            = NULL,
  file_name    = "Tutorial",
  plot         = TRUE
)
```

[`CellTFusion()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/CellTFusion.md)
when `cancer_type` is given:

``` r
res <- CellTFusion(raw.counts = raw.counts, cancer_type = "skcm")

res$Metaprograms_reference  # meta-program reference used
```

---
title: "Statistical analysis"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Statistical analysis}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(CellTFusion)
```

This tutorial shows how to test associations between `CellTFusion` features — latent factors, TF modules or cell groups — and clinical variables. It uses the result of `CellTFusion()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
raw.counts <- CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto
traitdata  <- CellTFusion::traitdata.tuto

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts  = raw.counts,
  normalized  = TRUE,
  return      = TRUE
)
```

## **Latent factors and clinical traits**

`scores.stat.analysis()` tests each latent factor against a clinical variable and saves a plot for every significant association in `Results/`. `scores` can be the output of `compute.latent_factors()` (`res$Latent_spaces`), a samples x features matrix, or a list whose first element is that matrix (e.g. `res$Cell_groups`). The samples are matched to the rows of `coldata` by row name (without row names in `coldata`, its rows must be in the order of the scores), and samples with a missing trait are left out. The trait must be categorical.

Available tests (`test`):

- `"wilcox"` — Wilcoxon rank-sum test (two groups).
- `"ttest"` — Welch's t-test (two groups, unequal variances).
- `"kruskal"` — Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn post-hoc tests (two or more groups).
- `"anova"` — one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc tests (two or more groups).
- `"fisher"` — Fisher's exact test, with scores split at the median into High/Low.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
  scores  = res$Latent_spaces,
  coldata = traitdata,
  trait   = "Best.Confirmed.Overall.Response",
  test    = "wilcox",
  pval    = 0.05
)
```

The result keeps only the significant features (its first element has no column if none is significant), and its element `Statistics` gives the test of every feature (statistic, p-value, adjusted p-value). Use `padj = TRUE` to correct the p-values for the number of features tested (Benjamini-Hochberg); it is `FALSE` by default. The individual tests (`scores.wilcox.test()`, `scores.ttest()`, `scores.kruskal.test()`, `scores.anova.test()`, `scores.fisher.test()`) can also be called directly with a list whose first element is the score matrix.

The factor scores themselves are in `res$Latent_spaces$Z`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
factor_scores <- data.frame(res$Latent_spaces$Z)
head(factor_scores)
```

## **TF modules and clinical traits**

`compute.metadata.association()` relates TF module scores to all clinical variables at once. The rows of `coldata` must be the same samples, in the same order, as the rows of the module matrix (an error is raised otherwise):

- **Numeric traits** are correlated with each module (Spearman by default, `corr_type = "pearson"` for Pearson) and shown in a heatmap, annotated for p-values at or below `pval`. For traits with missing values, each p-value uses the number of samples with both values. Numeric columns are treated as continuous: convert number-coded categories (e.g. a stage coded 1 to 4) to factor to test them as groups.
- **Categorical traits** (text, factor and TRUE/FALSE columns) are tested with one-way ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc tests when `plot_grid = TRUE`, and saved as boxplot grids with one panel per significant module.

Traits that cannot be tested are skipped with a message: numeric traits without variation, and categorical traits with a single level or with one value per sample (e.g. a sample identifier). Use `padj = TRUE` to correct the p-values for multiple testing across the modules, for each trait (Benjamini-Hochberg).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
  scores = res$TF_network[[1]],
  coldata     = traitdata,
  pval        = 0.05,
  file_name   = "Tutorial",
  plot_grid   = TRUE
)

assoc$correlation  # module-trait correlations (numeric traits)
assoc$p_value      # their p-values
assoc$anova        # ANOVA of every module for every categorical trait
```

## **TF modules and pathways**

`compute.modules.relationship()` correlates two matrices of continuous features over the same samples, for example TF modules and pathway activities (Spearman by default, `corr_type = "pearson"` for Pearson), and saves a heatmap of the significant correlations. It is for numeric variables only; use `compute.metadata.association()` for categorical ones. With `plot_grid = TRUE`, a scatter plot is also drawn for the significant pairs (the 100 strongest at most).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rel <- compute.modules.relationship(
  matA      = res$TF_network[[1]],
  matB      = res$Pathways_scores,
  file_name = "Pathways_vs_TF_modules"
)

rel$correlation  # correlations (TF modules x pathways)
rel$p_value      # their p-values
rel$significant  # for each TF module, the pathways significantly correlated with it
```

## **Survival analysis**

`compute.survival.analysis()` compares Kaplan-Meier survival curves with a log-rank test (packages `survival`, `survminer` and `gridExtra`). It works in two modes:

1. **Predefined groups** (`group_column`) — e.g. a clinical risk group or a cluster assignment in the clinical data.
2. **Feature screening** (`scores`) — e.g. `res$Latent_spaces$Z`. Each feature is split into High/Low at a quantile (`quantile_cutoff`), and the features with a significant log-rank test (`pval`, optionally corrected with `padj = TRUE`) are returned, with a `Statistics` table giving the test of every feature. Samples without a value for `group_column` are left out. The rows of `features` must be the same samples, in the same order, as the rows of the clinical data.

Both modes need a time-to-event column and an event column (1 = event, 0 = censored) in the clinical data. The tutorial `traitdata` includes the overall survival of the patients: `os` (months) and `censOS` (1 = death, 0 = censored).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Predefined groups
surv_group <- compute.survival.analysis(
  coldata       = traitdata,
  time_column   = "os",
  event_column  = "censOS",
  group_column  = "Best.Confirmed.Overall.Response",
  file_name     = "Tutorial"
)

surv_group$p_value     # log-rank p-value
surv_group$median_PFS  # median survival per group (column name kept from the function output)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Feature screening on latent factors
surv_factors <- compute.survival.analysis(
  coldata       = traitdata,
  time_column   = "os",
  event_column  = "censOS",
  scores        = res$Latent_spaces$Z,
  pval          = 0.05,
  quantile_cutoff = 0.5,   # median split; e.g. 0.75 for top quartile vs rest
  file_name     = "Tutorial"
)
```

A Kaplan-Meier plot with a risk table is saved (always for predefined groups, and for every significant feature in feature screening) to `Results/SurvPlot_<group-or-feature>_<file_name>.svg` (`Results/SurvPlot_<group-or-feature>.svg` without `file_name`).

---
title: "multideconv"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{multideconv}

---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

`multideconv` is an integrative pipeline for combining first- and second-generation cell type deconvolution methods from bulk RNA-seq data, as described in [Hurtado et al., 2025](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.04.29.651220v2.article-info).

## Installation

To avoid GitHub API rate limit issues, set up a Personal Access Token (PAT) before installing:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
usethis::create_github_token()
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Install `multideconv` from GitHub:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv")
```

## Tutorials

Step-by-step tutorials are available in the **Articles** section of the navigation bar:

- **Deconvolution with default methods** — run first-generation deconvolution and access built-in signatures
- **Cell type subgroup analysis** — derive cell-type subgroups and build a deconvolution dictionary
- **Single-cell deconvolution** — construct metacells and apply second-generation methods
- **Pseudo-bulk profiles and benchmarking** — create pseudo-bulk data, generate custom signatures, and benchmark performance
- **Machine learning workflows** — use subgroup features in cross-validated ML models

## Citation

If you use `multideconv` in a scientific publication, please cite:

> Hurtado, M., Essabbar, A., Khajavi, L., & Pancaldi, V. (2025). *multideconv – Integrative pipeline for cell type deconvolution from bulk RNAseq using first and second generation methods.* bioRxiv. <https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.04.29.651220>

1	---
2	title: "Deconvolution with default methods"
3	output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
4	vignette: >
5	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Deconvolution with default methods}
6	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
7	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
8	---
9	
10	```{r, include = FALSE}
11	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
12	  collapse = TRUE,
13	  comment = "#>"
14	)
15	```
16	
17	```{r setup}
18	library(multideconv)
19	```
20	
21	## **Deconvolution with default methods**
22	
23	The basic function is to perform cell type deconvolution using six default methods (`quanTIseq`, `DeconRNASeq`, `CIBERSORTx`, `EpiDISH`, `DWLS`, `MOMF`) and nine default signatures (see paper [Hurtado et al., 2025](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.04.29.651220v2.article-info)). The function accepts either raw counts or TPM-normalized counts as input (with genes as SYMBOL).
24	
25	**NOTE:** If you plan to use `CIBERSORTx`, you must provide your credentials (see README for details). The resulting deconvolution matrix is automatically saved in the `Results/` directory.
26	
27	The output includes all combinations of deconvolution features, method-signature-cell type.
28	
29	```{r, eval = FALSE}
30	bulk = multideconv::raw_counts
31	deconv = compute.deconvolution(raw.counts = bulk, 
32	                               methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", 
33	                                           "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS","MOMF"), 
34	                               normalized = TRUE, 
35	                               return = TRUE, 
36	                               file_name = "Tutorial")
37	```
38	
39	To run only specific signatures, use the `signatures_select` argument. If `NULL` (default), all available signatures (package + custom from `Results/custom_signatures/`) are used:
40	
41	```{r, eval = FALSE}
42	deconv = compute.deconvolution(raw.counts = bulk,
43	                               methods = c("Quantiseq", "DeconRNASeq"),
44	                               normalized = TRUE,
45	                               signatures_select = c("BPRNACan", "LM22"),
46	                               return = TRUE,
47	                               file_name = "Tutorial")
48	```
49	
50	To speed up computation, `multideconv` supports parallelization. Set `doParallel = TRUE` and specify the number of workers based on your system's resources:
51	
52	```{r, eval = FALSE}
53	deconv = compute.deconvolution(raw.counts = bulk, 
54	                               methods = "DWLS", 
55	                               normalized = TRUE, 
56	                               return = TRUE, 
57	                               file_name = "Tutorial", 
58	                               doParallel = TRUE, 
59	                               workers = 3)
60	```
61	
62	Once deconvolution is complete, pass the result to `compute.deconvolution.analysis()` to reduce redundancy, group correlated features into subgroups, and (optionally) correct for batch/cohort effects — see the [Cell type subgroup analysis](a4_subgroups.html) article for a full walkthrough including the `batch` parameter and pathway characterisation with `compute.subgroup.pathways()`.
63	
64	## **Cell type signatures**
65	
66	In order to access the default signatures `multideconv` provides, you can do the following:
67	
68	To list all signatures
69	
70	```{r}
71	path <- system.file("signatures/", package = "multideconv")
72	list.files(path)
73	```
74	
75	To access a specific signature
76	
77	```{r}
78	signature = read.delim(paste0(path, "CBSX-Melanoma-scRNAseq.txt"))
79	head(signature)
80	```
81


## **Deconvolution with default methods**

The basic function is to perform cell type deconvolution using six default methods (`quanTIseq`, `DeconRNASeq`, `CIBERSORTx`, `EpiDISH`, `DWLS`, `MOMF`) and nine default signatures (see paper [Hurtado et al., 2025](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.04.29.651220v2.article-info)). The function accepts either raw counts or TPM-normalized counts as input (with genes as SYMBOL).

**NOTE:** If you plan to use `CIBERSORTx`, you must provide your credentials (see README for details). The resulting deconvolution matrix is automatically saved in the `Results/` directory.

The output includes all combinations of deconvolution features, method-signature-cell type.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bulk = multideconv::raw_counts
deconv = compute.deconvolution(raw.counts = bulk, 
                               methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", 
                                           "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS","MOMF"), 
                               normalized = TRUE, 
                               return = TRUE, 
                               file_name = "Tutorial")
```

To run only specific signatures, use the `signatures_select` argument. If `NULL` (default), all available signatures (package + custom from `Results/custom_signatures/`) are used:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
deconv = compute.deconvolution(raw.counts = bulk,
                               methods = c("Quantiseq", "DeconRNASeq"),
                               normalized = TRUE,
                               signatures_select = c("BPRNACan", "LM22"),
                               return = TRUE,
                               file_name = "Tutorial")
```

To speed up computation, `multideconv` supports parallelization. Set `doParallel = TRUE` and specify the number of workers based on your system's resources:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
deconv = compute.deconvolution(raw.counts = bulk, 
                               methods = "DWLS", 
                               normalized = TRUE, 
                               return = TRUE, 
                               file_name = "Tutorial", 
                               doParallel = TRUE, 
                               workers = 3)
```

Once deconvolution is complete, pass the result to `compute.deconvolution.analysis()` to reduce redundancy, group correlated features into subgroups, and (optionally) correct for batch/cohort effects — see the [Cell type subgroup analysis](a4_subgroups.html) article for a full walkthrough including the `batch` parameter and pathway characterisation with `compute.subgroup.pathways()`.

## **Cell type signatures**

In order to access the default signatures `multideconv` provides, you can do the following:

To list all signatures

```{r}
path <- system.file("signatures/", package = "multideconv")
list.files(path)
```

To access a specific signature

```{r}
signature = read.delim(paste0(path, "CBSX-Melanoma-scRNAseq.txt"))
head(signature)
```

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
suppressMessages(library(CellTFusion))

work_dir <- "/home/marcelo.hurtado/Documents/tme_analysis/2cbab8b568/work"
setwd(work_dir)

## ---- Load data ----
expr <- read.table("data/Gide_log2TPM.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
expr <- as.matrix(expr)

coldata_all <- read.table("data/colData_all.txt", header = TRUE, sep = " ",
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
coldata <- coldata_all[coldata_all$Cohort == "Gide", ]
rownames(coldata) <- make.names(coldata$Sample_id)

colnames(expr) <- make.names(colnames(expr))
expr <- expr[, rownames(coldata)]

# log2(TPM + 1) -> TPM (CellTFusion requires non-log TPM when normalized = FALSE)
tpm <- (2^expr) - 1
tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0

coldata$Response <- factor(coldata$Response, levels = c("NR", "R"))
coldata$Therapy  <- factor(coldata$Therapy)

## ---- Run CellTFusion pipeline (Gide cohort, melanoma) ----
setwd(file.path(work_dir, "results"))

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = tpm,
  normalized     = FALSE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"),
  do_parallel    = TRUE,
  workers        = 8,
  cancer_type    = "skcm",
  file_name      = "Gide",
  seed           = 123
)

saveRDS(res, "CellTFusion_Gide_result.rds")

## ---- TME states (factor -> meta-program / TME subtype mapping) ----
tme_states <- res$TME_states$factor_mapping
write.csv(tme_states, "TME_states_factor_mapping.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(res$TME_states$reference, "TME_metaprograms_reference_used.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Association of latent factors (TME states) with immunotherapy response ----
sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
  scores    = res$Latent_spaces,
  coldata   = coldata,
  trait     = "Response",
  test      = "wilcox",
  pval      = 0.05,
  padj      = TRUE,
  file_name = "Gide_Response"
)

write.csv(sig_factors$Statistics, "LatentFactors_vs_Response_stats.csv")
saveRDS(sig_factors, "LatentFactors_vs_Response.rds")

## ---- Combine TME state annotation with the Response statistics ----
stats_df <- sig_factors$Statistics
stats_df$factor <- rownames(stats_df)
summary_tbl <- merge(tme_states, stats_df, by = "factor", all.x = TRUE)
summary_tbl <- summary_tbl[order(summary_tbl$p_value), ]
write.csv(summary_tbl, "TME_states_vs_Response_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Also relate the underlying TF modules to Response (supporting evidence) ----
tf_assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
  scores    = res$TF_network[[1]],
  coldata   = coldata[, c("Response", "Therapy")],
  pval      = 0.05,
  file_name = "Gide",
  plot_grid = TRUE
)
saveRDS(tf_assoc, "TFmodules_vs_clinical.rds")

cat("\n\n================ DONE ================\n")
cat("Latent factors significantly associated with Response (wilcox, p<0.05):\n")
print(summary_tbl[summary_tbl$p_value < 0.05, c("factor", "best_MP", "TME_subtype", "statistic", "p_value", "p_adj")])

#' Build the result of a score-trait test
#'
#' Internal helper of the \code{scores.*} tests: adjusts the p-values, selects the significant features and returns
#' the significant part of \code{scores} with a table of the tests of all features.
#'
#' @param input The output of \code{prepare_trait_test()}.
#' @param statistic Numeric vector with the test statistic of each feature.
#' @param p Numeric vector with the p-value of each feature.
#' @param test Character. Name of the test.
#' @param statistic_name Character. Name of the statistic (e.g. "t").
#' @param pval Numeric. Significance threshold for the adjusted p-values.
#' @param padj Logical. If TRUE, the p-values are adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg method.
#'
#' @return A list with \code{result} (see the \code{scores.*} tests), \code{sig} (indices of the significant
#'   features) and \code{adjusted_text} (adjusted p-value of each feature for the plot subtitles, empty without
#'   adjustment).
#'
#' @keywords internal
finish_trait_test = function(input, statistic, p, test, statistic_name, pval, padj){
  if (!isTRUE(padj) && !isFALSE(padj)) stop("padj must be TRUE or FALSE")
  scores = input$scores
  features = colnames(input$X)
  p_adjusted = stats::p.adjust(p, method = if (padj) "BH" else "none")
  sig = which(!is.na(p_adjusted) & p_adjusted <= pval)

  statistics = data.frame(feature = features, test = test, statistic_name = statistic_name, statistic = statistic,
                          p_value = p, p_adjusted = p_adjusted, significant = seq_along(features) %in% sig,
                          stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  result = list()
  result[[1]] = scores[[1]][, sig, drop = FALSE]
  if (length(scores) >= 2) result[[2]] = scores[[2]][sig]
  if (length(scores) >= 3) result[[3]] = scores[[3]][sig]
  if (!is.null(names(scores))) names(result) = names(scores)[seq_along(result)]
  result[["Statistics"]] = statistics

  threshold = paste0(if (padj) "adjusted p-value (BH)" else "p-value", " <= ", pval)
  if (length(sig) == 0) {
    message("No significant feature after ", test, " (", threshold, ")")
  } else {
    message(length(sig), " significant feature(s) after ", test, " (", threshold, "): ",
            paste(utils::head(features[sig], 10), collapse = ", "), if (length(sig) > 10) ", ...")
  }

  # Adjusted p-value for the plot subtitles (empty without adjustment)
  adjusted_text = if (!padj) rep("", length(p)) else
    paste0(" | adjusted p (BH) ", ifelse(p_adjusted < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste0("= ", round(p_adjusted, 4))))

  list(result = result, sig = sig, adjusted_text = adjusted_text)
}

     bottom on the right, next to their cell group. The edge between a
     cell group and a feature is the CCA coefficient of the feature in
     the cell group score (‘xcoef’ in ‘Weights’, on the z-scored

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
suppressMessages(library(CellTFusion))

work_dir <- "/home/marcelo.hurtado/Documents/tme_analysis/2cbab8b568/work"
setwd(work_dir)

## ---- Load data ----
expr <- read.table("data/Gide_log2TPM.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
expr <- as.matrix(expr)

coldata_all <- read.table("data/colData_all.txt", header = TRUE, sep = " ",
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
coldata <- coldata_all[coldata_all$Cohort == "Gide", ]
rownames(coldata) <- make.names(coldata$Sample_id)

colnames(expr) <- make.names(colnames(expr))
expr <- expr[, rownames(coldata)]

# log2(TPM + 1) -> TPM (CellTFusion requires non-log TPM when normalized = FALSE)
tpm <- (2^expr) - 1
tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0

coldata$Response <- factor(coldata$Response, levels = c("NR", "R"))
coldata$Therapy  <- factor(coldata$Therapy)

## ---- Run CellTFusion pipeline (Gide cohort, melanoma) ----
setwd(file.path(work_dir, "results"))

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = tpm,
  normalized     = FALSE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"),
  do_parallel    = TRUE,
  workers        = 8,
  cancer_type    = "skcm",
  file_name      = "Gide",
  seed           = 123
)

saveRDS(res, "CellTFusion_Gide_result.rds")

## ---- TME states (factor -> meta-program / TME subtype mapping) ----
tme_states <- res$TME_states$factor_mapping
write.csv(tme_states, "TME_states_factor_mapping.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(res$TME_states$reference, "TME_metaprograms_reference_used.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Association of latent factors (TME states) with immunotherapy response ----
sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
  scores    = res$Latent_spaces,
  coldata   = coldata,
  trait     = "Response",
  test      = "wilcox",
  pval      = 0.05,
  padj      = TRUE,
  file_name = "Gide_Response"
)

write.csv(sig_factors$Statistics, "LatentFactors_vs_Response_stats.csv")
saveRDS(sig_factors, "LatentFactors_vs_Response.rds")

## ---- Combine TME state annotation with the Response statistics ----
stats_df <- sig_factors$Statistics
stats_df$factor <- rownames(stats_df)
summary_tbl <- merge(tme_states, stats_df, by = "factor", all.x = TRUE)
summary_tbl <- summary_tbl[order(summary_tbl$p_value), ]
write.csv(summary_tbl, "TME_states_vs_Response_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Also relate the underlying TF modules to Response (supporting evidence) ----
tf_assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
  scores    = res$TF_network[[1]],
  coldata   = coldata[, c("Response", "Therapy")],
  pval      = 0.05,
  file_name = "Gide",
  plot_grid = TRUE
)
saveRDS(tf_assoc, "TFmodules_vs_clinical.rds")

cat("\n\n================ DONE ================\n")
cat("Latent factors significantly associated with Response (wilcox, p<0.05):\n")
print(summary_tbl[summary_tbl$p_value < 0.05, c("factor", "best_MP", "TME_subtype", "statistic", "p_value", "p_adj")])

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     This function tests for associations between transcription factor
     (TF) module scores and available clinical traits. Numeric traits
     are correlated with each module (Pearson or Spearman) and shown as
     a heatmap. If ‘plot_grid = TRUE’, categorical traits (text, factor
     and TRUE/FALSE columns) are additionally tested with one-way ANOVA
     (Tukey HSD post-hoc) and shown as boxplot grids. All plots are
     saved in the Results/ directory, and the tables with the results
     are returned.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     compute.metadata.association(
       scores,
       coldata,
       pval = 0.05,
       corr_type = "spearman",
       file_name = NULL,
       ncol_grid = NULL,
       plot_grid = FALSE,
       padj = FALSE
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

  scores: A numeric matrix or data frame of TF module scores across
          samples. Typically the first element (TFs module matrix) of
          the output from ‘compute.WTCNA()’. Rows represent samples,
          columns represent TF modules.

 coldata: A data frame containing clinical traits (both categorical and
          numerical) for the same samples. Rows must be the same
          samples, in the same order, as the rows of ‘scores’ (checked
          by name; an error is raised otherwise). Numeric columns are
          treated as continuous: convert number-coded categories (e.g.
          a stage coded 1 to 4) to factor to test them as groups.

    pval: A numeric threshold (default = 0.05) to determine statistical
          significance (p-value, or adjusted p-value, ‘<= pval’). Only
          associations with (adjusted) p-values below this threshold
          are annotated in the heatmap or drawn as boxplots.

corr_type: Correlation used for the numeric traits: ‘"spearman"’
          (default) or ‘"pearson"’.

file_name: Optional character suffix of the names of the saved plots
          (‘NULL’ by default: no suffix).

ncol_grid: Integer. Number of columns in the grid of association
          boxplots. If ‘NULL’ (default), it is set to the ceiling of
          the square root of the number of panels.

plot_grid: Logical; if TRUE, tests categorical traits with ANOVA and
          saves boxplot grids. Default is FALSE.

    padj: Logical; if TRUE, the p-values are corrected for multiple
          testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg method, across the
          modules for each trait, and the adjusted p-values are
          compared with ‘pval’. Default is FALSE.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     Traits that cannot be tested are skipped with a message: numeric
     traits without variation, and categorical traits with a single
     level or with as many levels as samples (e.g. a sample
     identifier). Categorical traits are only analysed when ‘plot_grid
     = TRUE’; a message lists them otherwise.

     The size of the figures is computed from their content (number of
     modules and traits for the heatmap, number of panels for the
     boxplot grids), and the y-axis of each boxplot panel from its
     data.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     Invisibly, a list with the results:

        • ‘correlation’: matrix of module-trait correlations for the
          numeric traits (modules x traits).

        • ‘p_value’: matrix of their p-values.

        • ‘p_adjusted’: matrix of their Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
          p-values (equal to ‘p_value’ with ‘padj = FALSE’).

        • ‘anova’: data frame with the ANOVA of every module for every
          categorical trait (‘trait’, ‘module’, ‘F’, ‘p’,
          ‘p_adjusted’); ‘NULL’ if ‘plot_grid = FALSE’.

     The elements are ‘NULL’ when there is no trait of that type. The
     following files are saved to the Results/ directory:

        • ‘TF.modules_metadata_<file_name>.pdf’: a heatmap of
          module-trait correlations for numeric traits (only
          associations with p-value <= ‘pval’ are annotated, with the
          correlation and its significance: * < 0.05, ** < 0.01, *** <
          0.001, **** < 0.0001).

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     Unified interface for testing associations between any score
     matrix and a clinical/experimental trait. Accepts cell group
     scores, NMF latent factors (output of ‘compute.latent_factors()’),
     or any samples x features matrix.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     scores.stat.analysis(
       scores,
       coldata,
       trait,
       test = c("fisher", "wilcox", "anova", "kruskal", "ttest"),
       pval = 0.05,
       padj = FALSE
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

  scores: A list, NMF output from ‘compute.latent_factors()’, or a
          score matrix (samples x features). When a list, the first
          element must be the score matrix; optional second and third
          elements (e.g. the output of ‘construct_cell_groups()’) are
          subsetted to the significant features and returned with their
          names.

 coldata: A data frame (or tibble) containing clinical or experimental
          metadata for samples. Must include the column specified in
          ‘trait’. Its rows are matched to the samples of the scores by
          row name; without sample names, they must be in the order of
          the scores. Samples with a missing trait are left out.

   trait: Character. The name of the column in ‘coldata’ representing
          the clinical or experimental trait to test against (e.g.,
          response, subtype, etc.). It must be categorical.

    test: Character. Statistical test to perform. One of:

            • ‘"fisher"’ - Fisher's exact test (scores binarised at
              median)

            • ‘"wilcox"’ - Wilcoxon rank-sum test (non-parametric,
              binary traits)

            • ‘"anova"’ - One-way ANOVA (parametric, two or more
              groups)

            • ‘"kruskal"’ - Kruskal-Wallis test (non-parametric, two or
              more groups)

            • ‘"ttest"’ - Welch's t-test (parametric, binary traits)

          Only one can be used per call; defaults to the first one
          (‘"fisher"’).

    pval: Numeric. Threshold for significance: a feature is significant
          if its (adjusted) p-value is ‘<= pval’ (default: 0.05).

    padj: Logical; if TRUE, the p-values are corrected for multiple
          testing across the features with the Benjamini-Hochberg
          method, and the adjusted p-values are compared with the
          threshold. Default FALSE.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     The function automatically calls the corresponding statistical
     test function based on the ‘test’ argument:

        • ‘scores.fisher.test()’

        • ‘scores.wilcox.test()’

        • ‘scores.anova.test()’

        • ‘scores.kruskal.test()’

        • ‘scores.ttest()’

     Each test produces both a statistical result and visual outputs
     (PDF plots) stored in the ‘"Results/"’ folder for the significant
     features. These visualizations include the relevant test results
     (p-values) annotated on the plots.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A list whose first element is the score matrix restricted to the
     significant features (no column if none is significant). Optional

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
suppressMessages(library(CellTFusion))

work_dir <- "/home/marcelo.hurtado/Documents/tme_analysis/2cbab8b568/work"
setwd(work_dir)

## ---- Load data ----
expr <- read.table("data/Gide_log2TPM.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
expr <- as.matrix(expr)

coldata_all <- read.table("data/colData_all.txt", header = TRUE, sep = " ",
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
coldata <- coldata_all[coldata_all$Cohort == "Gide", ]
rownames(coldata) <- make.names(coldata$Sample_id)

colnames(expr) <- make.names(colnames(expr))
expr <- expr[, rownames(coldata)]

# log2(TPM + 1) -> TPM (CellTFusion requires non-log TPM when normalized = FALSE)
tpm <- (2^expr) - 1
tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0

coldata$Response <- factor(coldata$Response, levels = c("NR", "R"))
coldata$Therapy  <- factor(coldata$Therapy)

## ---- Run CellTFusion pipeline (Gide cohort, melanoma) ----
setwd(file.path(work_dir, "results"))

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = tpm,
  normalized     = FALSE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"),
  do_parallel    = TRUE,
  workers        = 8,
  file_name      = "Gide",
  seed           = 123
)

saveRDS(res, "CellTFusion_Gide_result.rds")

## ---- TME states = NMF latent factors, annotated by their cell niches ----
# (Latent_spaces$Z: samples x factors; Cells_niches: top contributing cell
# groups/deconvolution features of each factor, used to interpret/name it)
write.csv(res$Latent_spaces$Z, "TME_states_latent_factor_scores.csv")
write.csv(res$Cells_niches, "TME_states_cell_niches_composition.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Association of latent factors (TME states) with immunotherapy response ----
sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
  scores    = res$Latent_spaces,
  coldata   = coldata,
  trait     = "Response",
  test      = "wilcox",
  pval      = 0.05,
  padj      = TRUE,
  file_name = "Gide_Response"
)

write.csv(sig_factors$Statistics, "LatentFactors_vs_Response_stats.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(sig_factors, "LatentFactors_vs_Response.rds")

## ---- Combine TME state (cell niche) annotation with the Response statistics ----
niches <- res$Cells_niches
top_cells_per_factor <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(niches, niches$factor), function(d) {
  data.frame(factor = d$factor[1],
             top_cell_groups = paste(unique(d$cell_group)[seq_len(min(3, length(unique(d$cell_group))))], collapse = "; "))
}))
stats_df <- sig_factors$Statistics
summary_tbl <- merge(top_cells_per_factor, stats_df, by.x = "factor", by.y = "feature", all.y = TRUE)
summary_tbl <- summary_tbl[order(summary_tbl$p_value), ]
write.csv(summary_tbl, "TME_states_vs_Response_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Also relate the underlying TF modules to Response (supporting evidence) ----
tf_assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
  scores    = res$TF_network[[1]],
  coldata   = coldata[, c("Response", "Therapy")],
  pval      = 0.05,
  file_name = "Gide",
  plot_grid = TRUE
)
saveRDS(tf_assoc, "TFmodules_vs_clinical.rds")

cat("\n\n================ DONE ================\n")
cat("Latent factors (TME states) significantly associated with Response (wilcox, p<0.05):\n")
print(summary_tbl[!is.na(summary_tbl$p_value) & summary_tbl$p_value < 0.05,
                   c("factor", "top_cell_groups", "statistic", "p_value", "p_adjusted")])

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
suppressMessages(library(CellTFusion))

work_dir <- "/home/marcelo.hurtado/Documents/tme_analysis/2cbab8b568/work"
setwd(work_dir)

## ---- Load data ----
expr <- read.table("data/Gide_log2TPM.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
expr <- as.matrix(expr)

coldata_all <- read.table("data/colData_all.txt", header = TRUE, sep = " ",
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
coldata <- coldata_all[coldata_all$Cohort == "Gide", ]
rownames(coldata) <- make.names(coldata$Sample_id)

colnames(expr) <- make.names(colnames(expr))
expr <- expr[, rownames(coldata)]

# log2(TPM + 1) -> TPM (CellTFusion requires non-log TPM when normalized = FALSE)
tpm <- (2^expr) - 1
tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0

coldata$Response <- factor(coldata$Response, levels = c("NR", "R"))
coldata$Therapy  <- factor(coldata$Therapy)

## ---- Run CellTFusion pipeline (Gide cohort, melanoma) ----
setwd(file.path(work_dir, "results"))

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = tpm,
  normalized     = FALSE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"),
  do_parallel    = TRUE,
  workers        = 8,
  file_name      = "Gide",
  seed           = 123
)

saveRDS(res, "CellTFusion_Gide_result.rds")

## ---- TME states = NMF latent factors, annotated by their cell niches ----
# (Latent_spaces$Z: samples x factors; Cells_niches: top contributing cell
# groups/deconvolution features of each factor, used to interpret/name it)
write.csv(res$Latent_spaces$Z, "TME_states_latent_factor_scores.csv")
write.csv(res$Cells_niches, "TME_states_cell_niches_composition.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Association of latent factors (TME states) with immunotherapy response ----
sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
  scores  = res$Latent_spaces,
  coldata = coldata,
  trait   = "Response",
  test    = "wilcox",
  pval    = 0.05,
  padj    = TRUE
)

write.csv(sig_factors$Statistics, "LatentFactors_vs_Response_stats.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(sig_factors, "LatentFactors_vs_Response.rds")

## ---- Combine TME state (cell niche) annotation with the Response statistics ----
niches <- res$Cells_niches
top_cells_per_factor <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(niches, niches$factor), function(d) {
  data.frame(factor = d$factor[1],
             top_cell_groups = paste(unique(d$cell_group)[seq_len(min(3, length(unique(d$cell_group))))], collapse = "; "))
}))
stats_df <- sig_factors$Statistics
summary_tbl <- merge(top_cells_per_factor, stats_df, by.x = "factor", by.y = "feature", all.y = TRUE)
summary_tbl <- summary_tbl[order(summary_tbl$p_value), ]
write.csv(summary_tbl, "TME_states_vs_Response_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

## ---- Also relate the underlying TF modules to Response (supporting evidence) ----
tf_assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
  scores    = res$TF_network[[1]],
  coldata   = coldata[, c("Response", "Therapy")],
  pval      = 0.05,
  file_name = "Gide",
  plot_grid = TRUE
)
saveRDS(tf_assoc, "TFmodules_vs_clinical.rds")

cat("\n\n================ DONE ================\n")
cat("Latent factors (TME states) significantly associated with Response (wilcox, p<0.05):\n")
print(summary_tbl[!is.na(summary_tbl$p_value) & summary_tbl$p_value < 0.05,
                   c("factor", "top_cell_groups", "statistic", "p_value", "p_adjusted")])

---
name: env-background-jobs
description: Long-running R/Python jobs launched with plain nohup+& get killed when the Bash tool call returns in this sandbox; must fully detach.
metadata:
  type: project
---

Backgrounding a long computation with `nohup cmd > log 2>&1 &` is not enough in this environment: the process (and any child worker processes it spawns, e.g. `parallel::makeCluster` PSOCK workers) gets killed as soon as the Bash tool call that launched it returns, even though `nohup`/`&` normally survive shell exit. The parent ends up as a zombie and orphaned children linger briefly then die too.

**Why:** the sandbox appears to tie process lifetime to the tool-call's process group/session rather than just the parent shell, so `nohup` alone doesn't protect against it.

**How to apply:** launch long jobs with `setsid nohup cmd > log 2>&1 < /dev/null & disown` to fully detach into a new session. Verify survival with `ps -ef` (PPID should become 1) after the tool call returns, and poll the log file / `ps` in separate Bash calls rather than a single blocking sleep+check embedded in the launch call.

---
name: celltfusion-version-gotchas
description: Installed CellTFusion R package (v0.0.1) lacks the newer TME-state/meta-program mapping functions shown in the GitHub docs, and parallel DWLS deconvolution OOM-crashes on this machine.
metadata:
  type: project
---

The CellTFusion package installed in the R library (`/home/marcelo.hurtado/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.3/CellTFusion`, version 0.0.1) is older than the dev docs/vignettes checked out at `~/Documents/CellTFusion` (which describe `compute_factor_gsea()`, `map_factors_to_metaprograms()`, `map_factors_to_TME()`, `derive_meta_programs()`, and a `res$TME_states`/`res$Metaprograms_reference` output). None of those functions exist in the installed namespace (`getNamespaceExports("CellTFusion")` confirms), even though `CellTFusion()`'s `cancer_type` argument is present — in the installed version it is only used for the ARACNE TF-collection path, not meta-program mapping.

**Why:** the GitHub repo had moved ahead of what was actually `pak::pkg_install`'d; always check `packageVersion("CellTFusion")` and `getNamespaceExports("CellTFusion")` before relying on vignette examples.

**How to apply:** in this installed version, "TME states" = the NMF latent factors from `compute.latent_factors()` (`res$Latent_spaces$Z`), annotated/interpreted via `compute_cells_niches()` (`res$Cells_niches`, giving each factor's top cell groups/deconvolution features). Also, `scores.stat.analysis()` in this version has **no** `file_name` argument (unlike the vignette). Separately, running `deconv_methods` with `"DWLS"` and `do_parallel = TRUE` reliably OOM-crashed the main R process on this 15GB-RAM/2GB-swap machine (workers ~1GB each orphaned as zombies); drop DWLS or run it sequentially (`do_parallel = FALSE`) instead. [[env-background-jobs]]

name: gide-cohort-data
description: Structure of data/colData_all.txt and data/Gide_log2TPM.txt (and sibling Riaz_log2TPM.txt) used for TME/immunotherapy-response analyses with CellTFusion.
metadata:
  type: project
---

`data/colData_all.txt` (336 rows) pools clinical annotation for several melanoma immune-checkpoint-blockade cohorts (Hugo, Gide, Riaz, ...) with columns `rna_id, Sample_id, Timing, Response (R/NR), Therapy (PD1 / CTLA4+PD1 / CTLA4 / PDL1 / PD1+KIR), Cohort`. Filter by `Cohort` to get a single study.

The Gide cohort: 73 samples, all `Timing == "Pre"` (baseline, pre-treatment), 46 R / 27 NR, split across `Therapy` PD1 (41) and CTLA4+PD1 (32). `Sample_id` values (e.g. `"10_PD1_PRE"`) match the column names of `data/Gide_log2TPM.txt` exactly (genes x samples matrix, values are log2(TPM+1), range ~0-14).

**Why:** needed to reconstruct non-log TPM (`2^x - 1`) before feeding into `CellTFusion(..., normalized = FALSE)`, which requires un-logged TPM.

**How to apply:** for any analysis of the Gide (or other) cohort from this combined colData file, subset `Cohort`, use `make.names()` on `Sample_id` to match the expression matrix's column names, and remember the values are log2(TPM+1), not raw TPM. See [[celltfusion_version_gotchas]] for the pipeline quirks encountered when running CellTFusion on this data.

input.content:
---
name: gide-tme-states-finding
description: CellTFusion result on the Gide melanoma cohort - 4 TME states (NMF latent factors) found, Factor1 (immune-enriched) significantly higher in immunotherapy responders.
metadata:
  type: project
---

Ran `CellTFusion()` (deconv methods Quantiseq/Epidish/DeconRNASeq, CollecTRI TFs, default WTCNA/cell-group/NMF settings) on the Gide melanoma cohort (73 pre-treatment samples, see [[gide-cohort-data]]). Results in `results/` (full pipeline object: `results/CellTFusion_Gide_result.rds`; package's own output folder nested at `results/Results/`).

NMF selected rank 4 (4 TME states / latent factors, all robust & non-redundant per bootstrap stability). Testing each factor's score against `Response` (R vs NR) with `scores.stat.analysis(test = "wilcox", padj = TRUE)`:
- **Factor1** is the only one significantly associated with Response: Wilcoxon W = 369, p = 0.0021, BH-adjusted p = 0.0082. Median score is 0 in NR vs 0.0064 in R (higher in responders).
- Factor1's top cell niches (`res$Cells_niches`) are dominated by lymphoid/myeloid infiltration features: B cells, memory B cells, plasma cells, CD4/CD8 T cells, NK cells, monocytes, M1 macrophages, activated dendritic cells — i.e. an immune-enriched TME state.
- Corroborating evidence at the TF-module level (`compute.metadata.association`): the "green" and "greenyellow" TF modules (the same modules underlying Factor1's cell groups) are also significantly associated with Response (ANOVA p = 0.0006 and p = 0.026 respectively).

**Why:** confirms the expected immunology: higher immune-cell infiltration (not fibrosis/stroma) pre-treatment associates with response to anti-PD1/anti-CTLA4+PD1 in this cohort, consistent with established TME subtype literature (e.g. Bagaev et al. immune-enriched vs fibrotic/depleted subtypes), even though this installed CellTFusion version can't auto-label factors with those subtype names (see [[celltfusion_version_gotchas]]).

**How to apply:** if asked to extend/validate this (e.g. on Riaz_log2TPM.txt, or with batch-mode across cohorts), reuse this same pipeline/parameter choices, and expect Factor1-like immune-enriched states to be the one worth testing first against response.

Ran `CellTFusion()` (deconv methods Quantiseq/Epidish/DeconRNASeq, CollecTRI TFs, default WTCNA/cell-group/NMF settings) on the Gide melanoma cohort (73 pre-treatment samples, see [[gide-cohort-data]]). ## Summary

I ran `CellTFusion` on the Gide melanoma cohort (73 pre-treatment samples from `data/Gide_log2TPM.txt`, matched to `Response`/`Therapy` in `data/colData_all.txt`). All outputs are in `results/` (pipeline object `CellTFusion_Gide_result.rds`, CSVs, and the package's own plots/tables nested under `results/Results/`).

**TME states found:** NMF identified 4 robust latent factors (TME states) from the cell-group scores (deconvolution × TF-module structure).

**Relation to immunotherapy response:** Testing each factor against `Response` (Wilcoxon, BH-adjusted):
- **Factor1 is significantly associated with response** (p = 0.0021, adj. p = 0.0082), with higher scores in responders than non-responders.
- Factor1's defining cell niches are an **immune-enriched signature** — B cells, memory B/plasma cells, CD4/CD8 T cells, NK cells, monocytes, M1 macrophages, activated dendritic cells.
- This is corroborated at the TF-module level: the same underlying modules ("green", "greenyellow") are independently associated with response (ANOVA p = 0.0006 and 0.026).
- Factors 2–4 showed no significant association with response.

Key result files: `results/TME_states_vs_Response_summary.csv` (factor stats + top cell groups), `results/TME_states_cell_niches_composition.csv` (full niche composition), `results/Results/Wilcoxon_Response_Factor1.pdf` (boxplot).

Two implementation notes worth flagging: the installed `CellTFusion` R package (v0.0.1) is older than its GitHub docs and lacks the meta-program/TME-subtype auto-annotation functions, so "TME states" here are the NMF factors annotated by their top cell-niche composition rather than named subtypes (e.g. "immune-enriched" is my interpretation of the composition, not a package-assigned label). Also, parallel DWLS deconvolution repeatedly OOM-crashed the run, so I used Quantiseq/Epidish/DeconRNASeq only.

The analysis is finished. Do not run anything else. Answer these questions about what you did, briefly and factually:
1. Input data: did you transform the expression values before using them (for example from log2 to linear TPM)? For which steps, and why?
2. Methods: which methods or functions did you run? Which available methods or steps did you skip, and why?
3. Parameters: which parameters did you set to a value other than the default, and why?

content.text:
**1. Input data transformation**
Yes. `Gide_log2TPM.txt` contains log2(TPM+1) values (range 0–14.04). `CellTFusion()` with `normalized = FALSE` requires un-logged TPM, so I converted with `tpm = 2^x - 1` (clipping any negative rounding artifacts to 0) before passing it in. No other transformation was applied — deconvolution, TF-activity, and pathway steps compute their own internal normalizations.

**2. Methods run / skipped**
Ran the full `CellTFusion()` wrapper: deconvolution (`multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` with Quantiseq, Epidish, DeconRNASeq), TF activity (`compute.TFs.activity()`, CollecTRI), TF co-activity modules (`compute.WTCNA()`), pathway activity (PROGENy), cell-group construction (`construct_cell_groups()`), NMF latent factors (`compute.latent_factors()`), cell niches (`compute_cells_niches()`), and clinical association (`scores.stat.analysis()` for latent factors vs. Response, `compute.metadata.association()` for TF modules vs. Response/Therapy).

Skipped:
- **CBSX (CIBERSORTx)** — needs user credentials, none provided; auto-skipped by the package.
- **DWLS** — attempted with `do_parallel = TRUE`, but it OOM-crashed the main R process twice (workers ~1GB each, machine has 15GB RAM/2GB swap, already near capacity). Dropped it entirely rather than risk a third crash.
- **MOMF** — not in `CellTFusion()`'s own default `deconv_methods` list, so never attempted.
- **`cancer_type` / meta-program / TME-subtype mapping** — the installed package version (0.0.1) doesn't export `compute_factor_gsea()`/`map_factors_to_metaprograms()`/`map_factors_to_TME()` despite the GitHub vignette describing them; confirmed via `getNamespaceExports()`. So I didn't get a subtype label (e.g. "IE"/"F") — I annotated factors manually from `Cells_niches` composition instead.
- **Survival analysis (`compute.survival.analysis()`)** — skipped, no survival/time-to-event columns exist in `colData_all.txt` (only `Response`, `Therapy`, `Timing`).

**3. Non-default parameters**
- `normalized = FALSE` (data was already TPM after my conversion, not raw counts).
- `deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq","Epidish","DeconRNASeq")` instead of the function default (which also includes CBSX, DWLS).
- `do_parallel = FALSE` (default) after the parallel DWLS crash — not actually a deviation since DWLS was removed, but I explicitly disabled parallelism.
- `seed = 123` — left at default, not changed.
- `padj = TRUE` in `scores.stat.analysis()` (default `FALSE`) — chose BH correction since 4 factors were tested against Response, to control multiple-testing inflation.
- Everything else (NMF rank search 2:15, `corr_mod = 0.9`, `min_module_size = 5`, `pval = 0.05`, `top_n = 5`, etc.) was left at package defaults.

**4. Problems encountered**
- Two full pipeline crashes during the DWLS-parallel deconvolution step: the main R process died (became a zombie/disappeared) while orphaned worker processes lingered, consuming memory until killed. `free -h` showed swap fully exhausted at the time. No `dmesg`/OOM log access to confirm the exact kill mechanism, but memory pressure during 8-way parallel DWLS is the clear proximate cause. Handled by removing DWLS and parallelism rather than retrying with fewer workers, to avoid a third failed run.
- Separately, the first two background-launch attempts (`nohup ... &`) were killed as soon as the Bash tool call returned, before DWLS was even reached. Handled by relaunching with `setsid nohup ... < /dev/null & disown` to fully detach the process into its own session.
- `scores.stat.analysis()` in the installed version has no `file_name` argument (unlike the vignette example) — caught before running by checking `args()`/help on the installed function, and removed that argument from my call.

**5. Checks performed before trusting results**
- Verified log2TPM value range (0–14.04, no negatives) matched the log2(TPM+1) assumption before converting.
- Verified all 73 Gide `Sample_id`s matched the expression matrix's column names exactly (`setdiff` empty) and that row/column ordering was aligned before passing data to `CellTFusion()`.
- Checked installed package version and exported function list (`packageVersion`, `getNamespaceExports`) against the newer GitHub docs before relying on vignette-described behavior, since they diverged.
- Confirmed the pipeline log showed "Everything done!" with no trailing errors, and that expected output files (TF matrix, cell groups, NMF stability plot, niche composition) were all written.
- Cross-checked the Factor1–Response association at a second, independent level (TF module ANOVA on "green"/"greenyellow" modules) rather than relying on the latent-factor test alone.
- Confirmed the direction of the effect (median Factor1 score 0 in NR vs. 0.0064 in R), not just the p-value, before describing it as "higher in responders."

**6. Limits / caveats**
- Only 3 of the 5 commonly-used first-generation deconvolution methods were used (no CBSX, no DWLS); results could shift somewhat with a fuller deconvolution ensemble.
- "Immune-enriched" is my descriptive label from inspecting Factor1's cell-niche composition, not a package-assigned, validated TME-subtype annotation (that functionality isn't available in the installed version) — treat it as an interpretation, not a formal classification.
- n=73 with 27 NR / 46 R is a modest sample size for a single factor's Wilcoxon test; the finding is statistically significant after BH correction but not independently validated on a held-out cohort (e.g. Riaz) in this run.
- NMF rank selection (4) and WTCNA module detection used default thresholds (`corr_mod = 0.9`, bootstrap `n_boot = 100`, etc.) — not tuned or sensitivity-tested for this specific dataset.
- No survival/PFS data was available, so I cannot say whether this TME state also relates to longer-term outcome, only to the binary R/NR label as recorded in `colData_all.txt`.
